indicators.note: crossing here is read as cross-wise, so the letters of the mountain range are crossed over into a new order

parts.note: taken as written, the anagram fodder

explanation.surface: A vehicle of old was taken over the Andes mountains.
explanation.walkthrough: 'crossing' looks like a journey over the mountains, but it signals the letters of ANDES rearranged; 'used' joins the definition to the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: A covered chair carried on poles by two bearers was a common way to travel in the 17th and 18th centuries.

indicators.note: a roundabout path is a twisting one, so the letters of the clue's first word are twisted into a new order

explanation.surface: Someone was sent the long way round.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both definition and wordplay: the letters of ROUTED rearranged give a word for a route taken in a roundabout way.
explanation.definitionFit: A diversion is an indirect route taken around an obstacle, which is exactly a path sent round the long way.

clue.text: In one sense the real thing, though spirit-like

indicators.note: the wanted word sits in the run of clue words one sense the real, starting at the last letter of sense

explanation.surface: Something seems genuine in one way, though ghostly in another.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' signals letters lying inside the phrase: the E ending 'sense' plus 'the real' run together.
explanation.definitionFit: Something light, delicate and unworldly, like a ghost or spirit, is described with this word.

clue.text: New York's out West from these scattered islands

indicators.note: scattered letters are thrown about, so the remaining letters are rearranged
out tells us that one piece is dropped from the city name, here the compass letter

parts.note: the city's name with its possessive S, giving the letters NEWYORKS

explanation.surface: Someone from New York heads west from a group of far-flung islands.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out' removes W from NEWYORKS, leaving NEYORKS, and 'scattered' rearranges those seven letters; 'from these' links to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The archipelago off the north-east tip of Scotland is a group of some seventy islands, often given a plural name.

indicators.note: in a down clue a piece written under another follows it, so the tension word comes after the motorway

parts.note: the M1 is Britain's main north-south motorway, written MI in crosswords
stress is strain or tension

explanation.surface: A female teacher is feeling the strain of driving on the motorway.
explanation.walkthrough: The M1 is the London to Leeds motorway; its 1 is read as the letter I. 'under' puts STRESS below MI in the down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: A schoolmistress is a woman who teaches, the old word for a female teacher.

clue.text: Little chap, you could say, ready to fight at short notice

definitions.text: ready to fight at short notice

explanation.surface: A small fellow is always spoiling for a fight.
explanation.walkthrough: Split as a phrase it is a 'minute' (tiny) man; as one word it is an American militiaman of the War of Independence, pledged to turn out at a minute's warning.
explanation.definitionFit: A tiny fellow is a very small man, and the colonial American militia were called up within moments of an alarm.

clue.text: Kind of work giving one little standing …

definitions.text: Kind of work giving one little standing …

parts.words: Kind of work giving one little standing
parts.note: describes a desk job in which the worker spends very little time on their feet, with standing also hinting at low status

explanation.surface: A lowly job gives a person little status in life.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Standing' reads as status, but the job is literally one done sitting down. The dots lead on to the next clue, which shows the same sitting.
explanation.definitionFit: Desk-bound work keeps a person seated for most of the day rather than on their feet.

parts.note: follows on from the clue before: a protest in which demonstrators occupy a building by remaining seated there

explanation.surface: A job proves the previous point.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Occupation' reads as a job, but it is the occupying of premises, and 'demonstrates' is what protesters do.
explanation.definitionFit: A protest in which people occupy a place and refuse to leave, sitting down in it, is this kind of occupation.

clue.text: Linen, not 26, in the crudest form

indicators.note: the wanted word sits in the clue words the crudest, from the final letter of the to the middle of crudest

explanation.surface: Linen that has not been processed is in its roughest state.
explanation.walkthrough: 26 is BLEACHED, so 'Linen, not 26' is the colour of unbleached linen. 'in' signals letters lying inside 'the crudest'.
explanation.definitionFit: This greyish-fawn shade takes its name from the colour of raw, unwhitened linen.

clue.text: Jean astride a horse in James I's time

indicators.note: a rider astride a horse has legs on either side of it, so the name sits on both sides of the other letters

parts.note: taken as written
a cob is a sturdy short-legged horse

explanation.surface: A woman named Jean rides a horse in the reign of the first Stuart king.
explanation.walkthrough: 'astride' reads as Jean on horseback, but it puts the name around the other pieces like a rider's legs. James I in Latin is Jacobus, hence the period name.
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin for James is Jacobus, so the period of his reign from 1603 to 1625 takes an adjective from it.

parts.note: describes a clipping scissored out of a newspaper, or a paper shape snipped out

explanation.surface: Someone clips an item from the newspapers.
explanation.definitionFit: A clipping or paper shape removed from a sheet with scissors is given this compound name.

clue.text: Fish a senior fellow takes to heart

indicators.note: the phrase senior fellow holds the wanted word at its centre, the end of senior joined to the start of fellow

explanation.surface: A senior college fellow is fond of a certain fish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'takes to heart' looks like the fellow being moved, but it means the phrase 'senior fellow' holds the fish in its middle: seniOR FEllow.
explanation.definitionFit: The ide, a freshwater carp-like species often kept golden in ornamental ponds, is also known by this name.

clue.text: The answer to what may happen tomorrow

definitions.text: The answer to what may happen tomorrow

parts.words: The answer to what may happen tomorrow
parts.note: asked what the future holds, the honest reply is that nobody knows for sure

explanation.surface: Someone asks about the future and gets a reply.
explanation.walkthrough: The stock reply to 'what will happen tomorrow?' is a shrug that the future cannot be predicted; it is also the title of a Shaw comedy.
explanation.definitionFit: The future is unpredictable, so the only true response to a question about it is that its outcome is unknowable.

clue.text: Their love affairs appear below average

definitions.text: Their love affairs appear below average

indicators.note: in a down clue a piece that appears below another follows it in the entry

parts.note: par is the normal or average level, as in feeling below par
amours are love affairs, usually secret ones

explanation.surface: A couple's romances are not up to much.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both wordplay and definition: illicit lovers are people whose love affairs are below par. 'appear below' puts AMOURS under PAR.
explanation.definitionFit: Illicit lovers conduct affairs that society regards as falling short of respectable standards.

indicators.note: something fashioned is shaped or made anew, so these letters are reshaped into another word

parts.note: the word with its possessive S counted as a letter
taken as written

explanation.surface: A lout's headgear is all the rage in a Moroccan city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fez' reads as the Moroccan city, but it is the flat-topped brimless felt hat. 'fashionable' rearranges BOORSHAT.
explanation.definitionFit: The brimless red felt cap with a tassel worn in parts of the Middle East and North Africa goes by this Arabic name.

clue.text: Plainly blessed cathedral city Welsh Jane is attached to

indicators.note: the Welsh name is joined on after the city, the two pieces placed side by side

parts.note: Ely is a small cathedral city in Cambridgeshire
Sian is the Welsh form of the name Jane

explanation.surface: A Welsh woman called Jane is devoted to a cathedral city where she clearly feels blessed.
explanation.walkthrough: ELY is a cathedral city in eastern England. 'Plainly blessed' reads as obviously happy, but it refers to the Elysian Fields, the plains of the blessed in Greek myth.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth the heroic dead lived in bliss on the Fields of the Blest, which gives an adjective for heavenly delight.

clue.text: Strike the flag at a Welsh university

parts.note: to lam is to hit or thrash
the Blue Peter is the flag flown by a ship about to sail, often called just the peter

explanation.surface: Someone takes down the flag at a college in Wales.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Strike the flag' reads as lowering it, but 'Strike' gives LAM and 'the flag' the Blue Peter.
explanation.definitionFit: St David's College in this small Ceredigion town is the oldest degree-awarding institution in Wales.

explanation.surface: Traditional cricket bowlers from the United States are being described.
explanation.walkthrough: The Derby is one of the five Classics of English flat racing, and Americans call a bowler hat a derby; 'bowlers' looks like cricket.
explanation.definitionFit: Epsom's famous horse race is one of the Classic races, and in the United States a round hard felt hat is named after it.

explanation.surface: An evenly balanced contest suits a relative.
explanation.walkthrough: An Aunt Sally is a fairground game of throwing at a dummy's head, hence any target of easy criticism; 'Aunt Sally' looks like a person.
explanation.definitionFit: An evenly matched contest is just and square, and a legitimate target for attack is one anybody may aim at.

explanation.surface: A fresh room is being described.
explanation.walkthrough: The '3' refers to the answer of 3 down, a word for spirit-like; both share the sense of lightness and insubstantiality.
explanation.definitionFit: A room with plenty of fresh breezes is breezy, and something light and delicate as a spirit is insubstantial in the same way.

explanation.surface: A nightclub is supplying a bit of seasoning.
explanation.walkthrough: One sense is a heavy spiked staff or ceremonial club; the other the spice made from the outer covering of the nutmeg.
explanation.definitionFit: A medieval weapon is a spiked bludgeon, and the lacy outer coat of nutmeg is dried and ground as seasoning.

clue.text: Suffering in court puts the seal on it

indicators.note: in tells us one piece sits inside the other, the pain within the court letters

parts.note: an ache is a dull, lasting pain

explanation.surface: Painful legal proceedings bring matters to a close.
explanation.walkthrough: 'puts the seal on it' reads as finishing something off; only 'the seal' defines, a mark of distinction. 'in' signals the container.
explanation.definitionFit: A signet's impression on a letter was a mark of authority, and the word now means prestige or a distinguishing stamp.

parts.note: a straight length of river between two bends, and also, read on its own, the verb to stretch out

explanation.surface: A length of river is being described.
explanation.walkthrough: Both senses are in play: 'Stretch' as a verb, to extend the arm, and the whole as a straight length of river between bends.
explanation.definitionFit: Boating people speak of the straight section of a river between two bends, and to stretch out an arm is to extend it.

clue.text: Anguish of a buck, we hear

indicators.note: we hear tells us the slang money word is spoken aloud and a word with the same sound is entered

parts.note: a buck is slang for a dollar

explanation.surface: A male deer is heard to be in distress.
explanation.walkthrough: 'buck' looks like a male deer, but it is slang for a dollar; 'we hear' gives a word that sounds the same.
explanation.definitionFit: Grief and sorrow, a poetic word for deep mental suffering.

parts.note: read literally as washed until white, rather than the usual sense of covering up a scandal

explanation.surface: Was an official scandal covered up?
explanation.walkthrough: 'Whitewashed' normally means concealing wrongdoing; the question mark asks us to read it literally as washed white.
explanation.definitionFit: Something treated with a whitening chemical or the sun has lost its colour and become pale, literally washed white.

parts.note: split into two words, an irritable remark, and a mention of road crossings such as the striped zebra kind

explanation.surface: Someone writes a grumpy comment about the stripy animals.
explanation.walkthrough: Taken as two words it is a cross (peevish) reference (note), or a reference about crossings; zebra crossings are striped pedestrian crossings in Britain. As one term it is a note in a book pointing elsewhere.
explanation.definitionFit: A note directing the reader to another passage in the same book is this kind of pointer.
